prompt.context: Your client is a large pharmaceutical distributor in a market primarily consisting of three main players. The three firms have a combined market share of 96%. The client has been growing via acquisitions, and it operates in four business segments which are all operated independently: (1) Drug Distribution is the core business representing 85% of sales — the client buys drugs from pharmaceutical firms and distributes them to hospitals, etc., covering both brand name and generic drugs; this area has historically low margins. (2) Manufacturing and distribution of medical products, including instruments, ER kits, and supplies. (3) Pharmacy Services is the 'other' category comprised mostly of acquisition targets with no other logical home; services include temporary staffing and owning/operating retail pharmacies. (4) Drug vending machines segment, which supplies machines to hospitals that distribute high-frequency drugs to aid nurse productivity. The client has a long history of profits, but for the past four quarters, profits, the company's stock, and employee morale have all been down. The CEO has called you in to provide an assessment of how to improve profits.
prompt.question: How would you approach this meeting? What areas would you look at to improve profits?

framework: Profitability = Revenue − Costs; examine both levers across all four divisions
Revenue side: pricing pressure in low-margin drug distribution, growth opportunities in other segments, cross-selling to shared clients
Cost side: identify shared cost buckets — Admin/Overhead, Purchasing, Manufacturing, Sales, Distribution — that are currently duplicated across siloed divisions
Organizational structure: assess whether the current siloed model prevents economies of scale and creates redundant functions
De-silo recommendation: consolidate shared functions into a matrix organization to reduce costs and leverage cross-divisional strengths

questions.prompt: Walk through the primary corporate-level cost buckets and explain what opportunities exist in each.
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies five cost areas (Admin/Overhead, Purchasing, Manufacturing, Sales, Distribution) and explains concretely why each is inefficient under the siloed structure and how consolidation would help. Key points: Admin/Overhead is separately run between divisions and is not scalable; Purchasing has scale benefits in maintenance, repair, and operations spending; Manufacturing is used by only one division (medical products) and is not a core competence — outsourcing is an option; Sales organizations run separately but sell to the same clients, so combination yields large benefit; Distribution facilities run separately across the country for each division, all at approximately 50% capacity — consolidation would dramatically improve utilization.

recommendation: This client is a textbook case for 'de-silo-ing' and creating a matrix organization
By operating under consolidated cross-division functional groups (Admin, Purchasing, Manufacturing, Sales, Distribution), the organization will run with a much more efficient cost structure
The matrix structure will also allow the company to leverage cross-divisional strengths to increase revenues
risks: Change management and cultural resistance from independently operated divisions
Integration complexity given acquisitions in Pharmacy Services with no common operational heritage
Risk of losing divisional focus or accountability in a pure matrix model
next_steps: Quantify cost savings in each functional bucket — especially distribution (currently ~50% capacity utilization) and sales (overlapping client coverage)
Assess feasibility of outsourcing manufacturing in the medical products division
Design the target matrix org structure with clear ownership and governance
Develop a change management and communication plan to address morale issues during transition
